# Slot census: how many heap objects are live at once

How many lifetime-id slots does a process need? The decision rests on one number per program, input and dataset
size: the exact whole-run peak of simultaneously live heap objects in any one process. This directory measures it
natively on x86 with an `LD_PRELOAD` tracer over established benchmark suites. Capstone is not involved, so the
programs' own allocation behaviour is measured, not a port's.

**The numbers are in [REPORT.md](REPORT.md)** (generated by `report.py` from `results/`, with the figures in
`figures/`). This file says how they were measured.

## Layout

    instrument   census.h           the counting rules every tracer shares (one place for realloc, fork, peaks)
                 slotcensus.c       the tracer (LD_PRELOAD)
                 ffcensus.c         the same census for Firefox, as a replace-malloc library (+ ffcensus-dump.py)
                 control.c          positive control (C, with a fork child that clears its environment)
                 control_cxx.cc     positive control (C++ new[]/delete[])
                 ffcontrol.c        ffcensus's positive controls (control.c's sequence and an arena sequence)
                 check-control.py   compares a control's expected counts with its census lines
                 slotins.c          instructions and allocations per process, a DynamoRIO client (+ slotins.cmake)
                 insctl.c           slotins's control: loops of known instruction counts, threads and a fork
                 check-instructions.py  compares insctl's instruction counts with what its loops must add
                 tracer.sh          sourced by every runner: start_pass (pass directory, tools, controls),
                                    measured (one measured command in either mode), record_cell (one cells.tsv row)
    runners      run-spec.sh        SPEC CPU2017 rate
                 run-parsec.sh      PARSEC 3.0
                 run-pyperformance.sh  pyperformance on CPython
                 run-quickjs.sh     Octane on QuickJS
                 run-firefox.sh     Speedometer 2.1 and 3.1 on Firefox Nightly (+ ff-speedometer.py, its driver)
                 run-ycsb.sh        YCSB on Redis and memcached (+ libevent.sh)
                 run-webservers.sh  nginx with wrk, Apache httpd with ab
                 run-postgres.sh    PostgreSQL with pgbench
                 run-rocksdb.sh     RocksDB db_bench
                 run-sqlite.sh      SQLite speedtest1
                 run-mimalloc-bench.sh  mimalloc-bench (allocator stress tests)
    analysis     summarize.py       one pass: per-process and per-cell peaks, verdicts; "no data" is an error
                 pack.py            packs a pass into results/<pass>/ (five files) with host paths removed
                 report.py          every pass in results/ -> REPORT.md, and figures.py's figures
                 suites.py          what a cell is: suite, program, dataset, class; the figures' suite columns
                 figures.py         figures/ (slots, rates, peak-rate) and their caption drafts
    data         results/<pass>/    one directory per pass, result lines only

## The suites

Every workload is a named benchmark in a configuration published before; the papers are named here and in each
runner's header.

| suite | runner | program, version | datasets | class |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| SPEC CPU2017 rate, 16 C/C++ benchmarks | run-spec.sh | installed kit, GCC 15 `-O2` | test, train, ref | application |
| PARSEC 3.0, 13 packages | run-parsec.sh | Internet Archive copy of the Princeton release, 8 threads | simlarge, native | application |
| pyperformance (default set) | run-pyperformance.sh | CPython 3.13.7, pyperformance 1.14.0, `--fast` | `PYTHONMALLOC=malloc` and `pymalloc` | application / hidden |
| Octane | run-quickjs.sh | QuickJS 2026-06-04, the Octane copy in its extras | the 15 benchmarks | application |
| Speedometer 2.1, 3.1 (Mesh, PLDI 2019) | run-firefox.sh | Firefox Nightly 161.0a1 | both versions | hidden (JS heap) |
| YCSB load + A + C (SoCC 2010) | run-ycsb.sh | Redis 7.2.16 `MALLOC=libc`, memcached 1.6.45 | 10^5, 10^6, 5x10^6 (AtomicDisk, FAST 2025), 1.6x10^7 (PVLDB 2020) records | application (Redis), hidden (memcached) |
| nginx + wrk (DangZero, CCS 2022) | run-webservers.sh | nginx 1.20.2, 16 workers, `wrk -t16 -c256 -d30s` | 64-byte file | hidden (pools) |
| Apache + ab (CRCount, NDSS 2019; pSweeper, CCS 2018) | run-webservers.sh | httpd 2.4.58, `ab -n 100000 -c 128` | 64-byte file | hidden (pools) |
| PostgreSQL pgbench (TPC-B-like) | run-postgres.sh | 17.6, 16 clients, 120 s | scale 1, 10, 100 | hidden |
| RocksDB db_bench | run-rocksdb.sh | v10.10.1 | 10^6, 10^7 keys | hidden (memtable arena) |
| SQLite speedtest1 | run-sqlite.sh | 3.22.0 | size 25..800, lookaside on and off | application / hidden |
| mimalloc-bench | run-mimalloc-bench.sh | commit 39138260, procs 8 | bench.sh arguments | stress |

The classes say what the allocator below would see:

- **application**: every heap object is a malloc, so the count is the number of objects.
- **hidden**: the program carves its objects from blocks it mallocs itself (memcached's slabs, PostgreSQL's memory
  contexts, RocksDB's memtable arena, nginx's and Apache's pools, SpiderMonkey's garbage-collected heap in Firefox,
  SQLite's lookaside, CPython's pymalloc). The census counts the blocks: the number of objects the allocator below
  sees with the program unmodified, not the number the program has, so it is a lower bound. The paired runs (SQLite
  lookaside off, `PYTHONMALLOC=malloc`, memcached's own item count) measure what is hidden.
- **stress**: allocator stress tests, reported apart from applications.

## How a pass runs

Every runner first builds the tracer and runs three controls. The C control (with a fork child) and the C++ control
must match their expected counts under the tracer, and the C control without the tracer (the negative control) must
fail its check. Any other outcome exits 75 before anything is measured. A runner then downloads or unpacks its
program, records the archive's sha256 in `provenance.txt`, builds it, and runs one **cell** per program and dataset.
Each cell writes its census lines (one JSON line per process at exit) and gets a verdict: SPEC's from runcpu's own
output validation, the others' from the program's exit status and, where the program reports one, its own check
(pgbench's failed transactions, Redis's DBSIZE, memcached's replies, speedtest1's TOTAL line). A cell's peak is the
maximum over its **measured processes**: the benchmark binary, not the shells, harnesses or validators around it.
Each runner's header comment says exactly which processes and what makes a cell valid.

Runner notes that change what is measured:

- **SPEC**: a config generated from SPEC's `Example-gcc-linux-x86.cfg` (label `census`, the system GCC, `-O2`,
  `-fcommon -fpermissive`, `-std=gnu++14` for C++, 502.gcc_r's `-fgnu89-inline -D_FORTIFY_SOURCE=0`, 526.blender_r's
  `-std=gnu99`, without which glibc hides `struct timespec` from its `threads.c`). runcpu exits 0 when a benchmark
  fails to build, so the build log's `Build errors` line goes into the provenance. SPEC's image validators carry the
  same label and are not measured processes.
- **PARSEC**: GCC 15 and glibc 2.43 reject parts of its 2009 code as written; each fix restores what the code was
  written against, and the runner's header states each. The gcc configuration gains `-std=gnu11` and `-std=gnu++11`,
  and the four warnings GCC 14 made errors are demoted again. bodytrack and facesim are C++98 code (`throw()` lists on
  destructors, a stream compared with 0) and get `-std=gnu++98`. dedup's bundled OpenSSL gets a `termio.h`
  compatibility header (glibc 2.43 dropped `termio.h`) and a `pod2man` that writes placeholder man pages (today's
  `pod2man` rejects its 2009 POD). ferret uses `HUGE`, which glibc dropped, and gets glibc's former value (FLT_MAX).
  x264's hand-written assembly is not position independent, so it links `-no-pie`. canneal's thread entry point falls
  off its end and GCC 15 lets it run into the next function: it gets `return NULL;`, the one source change. facesim
  crashes at every optimisation level from `-O1` and runs at `-O0` (three single flags were tried, none suffices),
  so it is built at `-O0`. swaptions uses PARSEC's `gcc-pthreads` configuration (its `gcc` one is the TBB variant,
  whose bundled TBB does not build). raytrace needs X11 development libraries the measuring hosts lack, and is not
  measured. The native inputs come from the only surviving copy, the Internet Archive's, which ends after
  1,014,297,656 of 2,429,601,226 bytes (two downloads stopped at that byte): the native inputs stored before the cut
  are intact (blackscholes, bodytrack, facesim, ferret, fluidanimate, freqmine, vips; streamcluster and swaptions need
  none), and canneal, dedup and x264 are measured on simlarge only. PARSEC has no output checks.
- **pyperformance**: the measured processes are pyperf's workers. An extra control holds 200,000 objects: with
  `PYTHONMALLOC=malloc` its peak must reach 200,000, with pymalloc stay below 20,000. Three benchmarks run their
  workload in a child of the worker (pyperf's `bench_command`: 2to3, python_startup, python_startup_no_site), and
  no child is recorded, so their peaks (82,332 to 82,379 with malloc) are the worker's: the interpreter and pyperf,
  not the workload.
- **PostgreSQL**: every postgres process is measured; a backend is a fork child, so its count starts at the live
  set it inherits from the postmaster.
- **YCSB**: YCSB 0.17.0 with its own Redis and memcached bindings, on a Temurin JDK 11 unpacked in the pass
  directory. YCSB exits 0 even when it rejects its arguments, so a phase counts only if every operation returned OK
  and the server holds exactly the loaded records afterwards.
- **nginx**: nginx clears its workers' environment, so the tracer reads its output path at start-up (the C control's
  fork child clears its environment to prove it), and a pass is valid only if all 16 workers reported.
- **Firefox**: Firefox allocates through its own mozjemalloc; on Linux its Nightly builds take a replace-malloc
  library's `replace_init` from a preloaded library. ffcensus counts in front of mozjemalloc, with its counters in a
  file mapped per process (Firefox ends its children without running exit handlers). Its function table is built
  from the headers of the exact Nightly changeset; the one C++-only entry is kept as a same-size slot and the slot
  count is checked against the header. It reads a process's name only before the sandbox applies (the content
  sandbox kills a process that opens a file).
- **mimalloc-bench**: sh6bench and sh8bench need a separate download and are left out, as are the tests that drive
  external programs (the application runners cover those).

The control program is built with `-fno-builtin`: at `-O2` GCC deletes a `malloc` whose result is unused and a
`calloc`/`aligned_alloc`/`realloc(NULL)` freed at once, and the first version of the control lost 3025 events that
way. The benchmarks are built normally, so an allocation the compiler removes is not an object and is rightly not
counted.

What the tracer cannot see: objects inside a program's own allocator (above), allocations made by `dlsym` while it
resolves the real functions (a 64 KiB static buffer), and processes that end in `_exit` or a signal (no line).
Cross-check: the SPEC ref peaks of 500.perlbench_r and 502.gcc_r agree with an earlier, separately written tracer
on the same host (1,252,835 and 1,069,978).

## Allocations per instruction

The second figure divides a cell's allocations by the instructions its measured processes executed. Both counts come
from the same run under DynamoRIO 11.3.0 (`SLOTCENSUS_MEASURE=instructions`, the slotins client), because some
benchmarks run for a fixed time or calibrate their loop counts (Octane, pyperf), so a run under instrumentation does
less work than the census run and a ratio across two runs would mix two amounts of work. slotins counts application
instructions per basic block into a per-thread counter and wraps the malloc family with the tracer's rules. Every
runner runs the same commands in both modes. The exceptions: PARSEC's instruction passes do not follow execs
(facesim's `system("mkdir")` otherwise starts the multicall coreutils under the name `libdynamorio`), and
pyperformance's run only pyperf's workers under DynamoRIO, through a wrapper in the venv, with the rest native.
Four pyperformance benchmarks have no instruction count: 2to3, python_startup, python_startup_no_site and dask start
subprocesses with `close_fds=True`, and under DynamoRIO 11.3.0 the child spins forever, with or without a client and
with or without `-no_follow_children` (`close_fds=False` and `os.posix_spawn` run, 2026-10-26).

Before measuring, an instruction pass runs `insctl`: a 2-instruction loop run 10^8 times must count 2 instructions
per iteration more than a run with none, to within 1,000 instructions, for one thread, four threads (two still alive
at exit) and a fork (the child counts its own loop and none of its parent's threads). A client built with
DynamoRIO's skip-thread-exit-at-exit option fails it. control.c and control_cxx.cc under DynamoRIO must match their
expected allocation counts. Cross-check: on SQLite speedtest1 the DynamoRIO allocation counts match the census's to
within 0.5%.

The third figure (`figures/peak-rate.pdf`) plots each run with both measurements as its instructions per heap
allocation (x, the inverse of the second figure's rate: the mean allocation interarrival time in instructions, the
measure Zorn and Grunwald use for allocation-intensive C programs, CU-CS-604-92, 1992) against its peak (y). Both
axes are log2 from 2^0 with one power of two as long on each, and y ends at 2^25, the slots of a 55-bit lifetime id
split into 25 slot and 30 generation bits. The figure draws no model: with i slot bits and g generation bits a slot
retires after 2^g uses, so a process with peak L can run out of slots only after (2^i - L) x 2^g allocations, and the
caption turns the closest run's margin into instructions and into years at 10^9, 10^10 and 10^11 instructions per
second (`figures.py`). The middle rate is above every measured RISC-V core we found (2026-10): CVA6 runs at up
to 1.7 GHz in 22 nm with an IPC of 0.82 to 0.99 (arXiv 1904.05442), the SG2044 at 2.6 GHz (arXiv 2508.13840), SiFive's
P550 at 1.4 GHz with an IPC above 2 on its best SPEC programs (Chips and Cheese). The years scale as 1/rate: a
process twice as fast, or a multi-threaded process whose threads share its ids on several cores, halves them. For
scale: Zorn and Grunwald's six programs allocated once every 295 to 3,273 instructions on average, and the most
allocation-intensive run here (pyperformance spectral_norm with `PYTHONMALLOC=malloc`) once every 573. Redis is not
in this figure.

## Running

    bash run-spec.sh ~/spec2017/SPEC17 <pass-dir> [test|train|ref] [benchmark...]
    bash run-parsec.sh <pass-dir> [simlarge|native...]     (archives in $SLOTCENSUS_CACHE)
    bash run-pyperformance.sh <pass-dir> [benchmark...]
    bash run-quickjs.sh <pass-dir> [benchmark...]
    bash run-firefox.sh <pass-dir> [2.1|3.1...]
    bash run-ycsb.sh <pass-dir> [records...]
    bash run-webservers.sh <pass-dir>
    bash run-rocksdb.sh <pass-dir> [keys...]
    bash run-postgres.sh <pass-dir> [scale...]
    bash run-sqlite.sh <pass-dir> [size...]
    bash run-mimalloc-bench.sh <pass-dir> [test...]
    SLOTCENSUS_MEASURE=instructions bash run-<suite>.sh ...   (not Firefox: mozjemalloc is not wrapped)
    python3 summarize.py <pass-dir>
    python3 pack.py <pass-dir> results/<pass>
    uv run --with matplotlib python report.py

Run them on a measuring host, not a workstation: SPEC ref takes about 15 minutes with all benchmarks in parallel,
and each server cell a few minutes.

## Results

`results/<pass>/` holds what `pack.py` writes, with the pass directory written `<PASS>` and the home directory
`<HOME>`, in five files:
- `provenance.txt`: what ran and how (for SPEC with the generated runcpu config).
- `cells.tsv`: one row per cell, its selector, verdict and the runner's note (for SPEC runcpu's verdict line, exit
  code and run time).
- `processes.jsonl`: the census line of every measured process, with its cell.
- `outputs.txt`: the program's own result lines where a server runner keeps them (YCSB's operation counts, for one).
- `control.txt`: every control's checker lines, expected against measured values.

Full build and run logs, the raw control records and every process a cell does not measure carry the host's paths or
nothing the report needs, and stay on the host. A pass is named `<date>-<what>-<host>`, all measured on
Xeon Gold 6230 hosts with GCC 15.2 and glibc 2.43. `report.py` lists any cell that is not valid under "Excluded
cells", with its reason.
